$about: 2026-08-06, the track round: the eight open failures in the backlog/cycle/board machinery, each reproduced against the live tree before anything was written. Reproductions ran against a copy of fixture:test-greenfield-core with the case's `given` planted into it, and against purpose-built minimal fixtures where the case describes a shape the greenfield repo does not carry. Every fix was then re-run against the same fixture, against the worked adopting repository (three closed cycles, one open, a populated pool, a live in-flight pointer row), and against the greenfield fixture untouched - a guard that only learned to fail is a guard that stopped letting correct repos through.

observations.evidence: Reproduced first, exactly as the 2026-08-05 re-verification described it. On a copy of the fixture, `split -> IMPL-3` (the invented spelling the template warns about, which the fixture actually carries) was replaced with the declared `split:IMPL-3`, and DEC-1's status set to `blocked:IMPL-2`. The shipped guard printed `cycle-guard: OK - 6 intent(s) across 3 place(s), each in exactly one, 1 live block(s)`, exit 0 - a block on finished work certified as live. cycle-guard.mjs now reads `split:<id>` as finished for the staleness check: the same fixture reports `DEC-1 (docs/backlog.md) is blocked by IMPL-2, but IMPL-2 was split and IMPL-3 carries what remains - the block no longer applies`, exit 1. Reading the status as finished without checking what it names would have opened a wider hole than it closed - three words in a cell retiring any row and disarming every block pointing at it - so the reference is checked too: a `split:` naming an id that exists nowhere, or naming the row itself, is a failure. A plain `split` with no reference is still not read as finished, matching how plain `blocked` stays legal. Five cases in tools/cycle-guard-test.mjs cover it in both directions, including that a sibling row's split does not make an unrelated live block stale.

Reproduced by the case's own procedure: `grep -n '^| id |' standard/docs/backlog.md` returned `| id | title | cap | persona | owner | assignee | size | why | DoD | status |` - ten columns, no source column, against three documents claiming every item has one (standard/docs/backlog.md's `Not this` list, add-to-backlog's front matter and its step 1). The ledger row now declares `source` between `why` and `DoD`, in both standard/docs/backlog.md and standard/docs/cycles/_template.md, so a row still moves between pool and cycle unchanged, and the status stays the last cell the guard reads. Five categories are declared - `onboarding`, `spec-delta`, `drift`, `decision`, `asked` - which also reconciles the pool's four with add-to-backlog's five; the cell carries the category and then where to point (`drift: spec-reconcile 2026-08-04`, `asked: #212`). The Definition of Ready requires it, and add-to-backlog's three automatic triggers each name the category they file under. docs/method/tracking-work.md carried the honest admission that no source field existed and that a column would close it if it started mattering; that paragraph now describes the column.

Reproduced by reading the rendered board in docs/method/tracking-work.md: three lanes, six OVR cards, and `grep -n blocked docs/method/tracking-work.md` matched exactly one line - in the Jira prose, nowhere in the figure. The fourth declared status had no rendering at all. The board keeps three lanes, which was already cycle-open's documented decision (a `blocked:<id>` row stays in `doing` and says what it is waiting on) rather than a call re-made here; what was missing was the figure demonstrating it. OVR-5 now sits in `doing` with a `blocked` tag, a red rule, and `waiting on NOTIF-6` on the card - a decision still in the pool, so the example also shows a block reaching from a cycle into the backlog. Verified in the generated output, not only the source: site/docs/tracking-work.html carries `waiting on NOTIF-6` and the `.bd-blocked` rule that styles it. cycle-open's read-back step now states that the board must show the id, and that dropping it or moving the row to `todo` loses the only fact the row was worth rendering for; specs/work-cycles/spec.md carries it as an acceptance criterion.

Reproduced on a purpose-built nine-commit history with two teams whose windows overlap (dispatch: Ada and Ravi, 2026-05-01 to 2026-05-20; billing: Mira, 2026-05-10 to 2026-05-31). cycle-close's prescribed `git log --oneline --since=<opened> --until=<closed> | wc -l` returned 7 and 6; listing the same windows with `--format='%ad %an %s'` shows dispatch's 7 includes Mira's two billing commits and billing's 6 includes Ada's and Ravi's two dispatch commits. Neither number is about the team that wrote it, which is the blending /timeline-update explicitly refuses. Scoped to each cycle's own assignee set - `--author='Ada' --author='Ravi'` and `--author='Mira'` - the same history gives 5 and 4, genuinely different and each the team's own. cycle-close now prescribes that, with the roster probe (`git log --since --until --format='%an' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn`) first so an assignee who maps to no git author is named rather than silently costing the count; verified that an unmatched `--author` leaves the count unchanged (still 5), which is exactly why the probe is a step. Two failure modes are now reportable rather than absorbed: a window returning zero commits (confirmed: the unscoped command returns 0 for an empty window with no complaint) and a repo with no usable author mapping, which records the repo-wide count labelled as repo-wide. The recorded line names its scope, and the cycle template's outcome comment asks for it.

Reproduced with all three planted at once - a `done` row still in the pool, a pointer row for a cycle closed three months earlier, and a pointer declaring 4 items against a cycle holding 2: `cycle-guard: OK - 4 intent(s) across 2 place(s), each in exactly one`, exit 0. Two of the three are now mechanical and the fixture fails, exit 1, reporting `docs/backlog.md still points dispatch at docs/cycles/dispatch/may.md, which is closed`. On that fixture only the stale pointer is reported: the count check is deliberately skipped once a pointer's cycle has closed, because the row itself should be gone and two messages for one fix is noise. The count check is proven on its own in the harness (4 declared against 2 held, on an open cycle). The mechanism: the pool's `## In flight` table is read, each row's `Cycle` cell must resolve to a cycle file this guard reads (markdown link or bare/backticked path, tried against the pool's directory, the root and `docs/`), that cycle must not be `closed`, and a non-empty `Items` cell must be a bare number equal to the cycle's real intent-row count. Staleness is keyed on the cycle being closed rather than on the pointer's age: a guard reading a clock is not reproducible, and `/cycle-close` removing the row is the rule the age was a symptom of. Deleting the row is not the way out - once the table carries any pointer row, an open cycle no row names is also reported. A pool whose table holds only the shipped template's blank row is not using it and is not checked, which is what keeps the untouched greenfield fixture passing. The third violation, a `done` row lingering in the pool, is deliberately NOT a failure: standard/docs/backlog.md licenses it in the same sentence that declares the vocabulary ("drop `done` rows on release, or let the Backlog.md tool archive them"), and a guard failing every such row would make that licence impossible to follow. Changing the licence is a product call the owner has not made, so it is recorded here rather than taken. The case's `then` asks for at least one of the three to be flagged; two are.

Reproduced: `grep -rn infra` across standard/docs/backlog.md, standard/docs/personas.md, add-to-backlog/SKILL.md and docs/method/tracking-work.md matched exactly one line - `(infra)` inside the commented-out example block in the pool template, visible only to someone reading the raw file. Nothing in prose, and nothing checks backlog personas mechanically, so the doc's own headline content category (documentation, spec and decision debt) was parked by its own Definition of Ready. standard/docs/backlog.md now carries a section stating the answer: internal work names `Maintainer (internal)` - anyone who has to work in this repo afterwards, person or agent - and says plainly that nothing checks this mechanically, which is why it is written down. The Definition of Ready notes the internal persona counts; add-to-backlog step 4 names it rather than leaving the author to invent one; the commented example row uses it instead of `(infra)`.

Reproduced by the case's procedure. add-to-backlog step 3 said `a stable, scoped id (SPEC-3, ADR-auth, DRIFT-2)` - type-scoped throughout; the worked examples in docs/method/tracking-work.md and docs/tree/docs-cycles.md use INV-3, NOTIF-6, SCH-9, PAY-2 - capability-scoped throughout; standard/docs/backlog.md line 84 mixed both inside one sentence, `id is stable (CAP-3, ADR-auth)`. One convention now, stated once, in the pool template: the id's prefix names the thing the item belongs to - the capability where there is one (INV-3, PAY-2), the artifact type where there is not (ADR-auth, DRIFT-2, SPEC-1). Both worked-example families are instances of it rather than rival conventions. add-to-backlog and specs/work-cycles/spec.md point at that sentence and say not to restate it (R4, one home); the guard's own header comment, which listed three type-scoped examples and read like a second convention, now shows both shapes and names where the rule lives.

Reproduced: an intent copied into a cycle with the pool copy renumbered (INV-9 in docs/backlog.md, INV-2 in the cycle) and the title cell kept identical gave `cycle-guard: OK - 3 intent(s) across 2 place(s), each in exactly one`, exit 0 - the guard keyed entirely on the first-cell id and never compared titles. It now groups by normalized title as well: markup stripped, whitespace collapsed, case-folded, so `Reassign an  active **route**` and `Reassign an active route` are the same work. The same fixture reports `"Reassign an active route" is one intent in 2 places under 2 ids: INV-9 (docs/backlog.md), INV-2 (docs/cycles/dispatch/august.md)`, exit 1. Three ways this could have been over-broad are held down by their own cases: it fires only across files (a pool listing two similar rows is not two places), only when the ids differ (an id clash is already reported and is not double-counted), and never on a title with no letter or digit (`-` identifies nothing). The one legitimate shared title - a `split:<id>` row and the remainder row it names, which /cycle-close creates and an author may reasonably leave worded the same - is exempt, and a third row under that title is not. The title column is found by its header name, falling back to the cell after the id. Both directions are in tools/cycle-guard-test.mjs, and the worked adopting repository's 28 intents across 5 places still pass unchanged.
